analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income and estate taxes with a 15% national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 10 cosponsors in August 2001, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, the estate and gift taxes, and several excise taxes, and replace them with a 15% national sales tax on nearly everything consumers buy. The Internal Revenue Service would be phased out by 2006, with states collecting the new tax for a 1% fee. Families would get a paycheck rebate covering the tax on spending up to the poverty level, and any future increase in the tax rate would require a two-thirds vote in the House or Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and the wealthiest households would gain the most: the income tax, including taxes on capital gains, and the estate and gift taxes would be repealed entirely, so large salaries, investment gains, and inheritances would go untaxed. Businesses would gain from exempt business purchases and transition credits. States would gain a 1% fee for collecting the tax, and families at or below the poverty line would get a paycheck rebate covering tax on spending up to the poverty level.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income, estate, and gift taxes and phases out the IRS after fiscal year 2005, ending individual income tax filing.
Provides a 'family consumption refund' that rebates the sales tax on spending up to the poverty level, delivered through paychecks.
Exempts purchases made for a business purpose and for export, and gives businesses transition credits for inventory and compliance equipment costs.
Lets homebuyers pay the tax on a principal residence in equal annual installments over 30 years instead of upfront.
Has states administer and collect the tax in exchange for a 1% administration fee, relying on existing state sales tax systems.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who buys goods and services would pay a new 15% federal tax on top of existing state sales taxes. Because lower- and middle-income households spend most of what they earn while wealthier households save and invest more, the tax would take a larger share of lower incomes; the rebate covers spending only up to the poverty line, and the estate tax repeal means large inheritances would pay nothing at all.

drawbacks.text: A 15% federal sales tax would be stacked on top of existing state sales taxes, bringing combined rates in many states above 20% on nearly everything consumers buy, including rent, utilities, and financial fees.

Consumption taxes take a larger share of income from households that spend everything they earn; the poverty-level rebate offsets the tax only up to the poverty line, leaving most working families paying a higher effective rate than before while the estate tax repeal wipes out taxes on the largest inheritances.
The bill repeals the estate and gift taxes entirely, so multi-million-dollar estates would pay no transfer tax at all.
It would tax wages paid by government employers and unregistered employers as taxable services, a burden that falls on public payrolls, while wages from registered active-trade businesses are exempt.
The requirement that a two-thirds supermajority in either chamber approve any rate increase would lock in the new tax structure against future correction.
A flat consumption tax replaces a tax code whose burden rises with income, converting a progressive system into a flat one with a partial rebate at the bottom.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's appeal is real: no income tax filing, no IRS, and a rebate protecting families at the poverty line. But the arithmetic runs the other way for most working households. Replacing an income tax that rises with earnings — and an estate tax paid only by the largest inheritances — with a flat 15% tax on everything people buy shifts the burden toward households that spend most of what they make, while households living off accumulated wealth, whose gains and estates would go untaxed, come out far ahead. The rebate softens the hit at the bottom but does nothing for the broad middle, and a 15% rate stacked on state sales taxes is a steep new cost on everyday purchases, including a first-ever federal tax on home purchases. The bill died without a hearing, so these tradeoffs were never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Billy Tauzin introduced the bill on August 2, 2001, with 10 cosponsors — 8 Republicans and 2 Democrats.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, and no vote in either chamber before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one's federal taxes changed: the existing income and estate tax system stayed in place, households never faced a new 15% federal sales tax layered on top of state taxes, and the tax preparation industry kept the income tax filing business the bill would have eliminated.

for.name: W.J. 'Billy' Tauzin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the income, estate, and gift taxes and replace them with a 15% national sales tax administered by the states.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair: Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 8 Republicans to 2 Democrats, but no vote ever occurred to show whether the fight would have divided by party.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate and gift taxes outright and ends all income tax, including on capital gains, while the replacement consumption tax falls most heavily on households that spend most of what they earn. The poverty-level rebate cushions the bottom but does nothing for households well above it.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and closing the IRS would eliminate the compliance and filing business built around the tax code — paid preparers, tax software, and accountants. The bill's death preserved that revenue.

Retailers would become collectors of the new federal tax, with monthly reporting, registration, and penalties, but would receive an administrative credit of at least $200 (or 0.5% of tax remitted) and a credit for 50% of new compliance equipment costs.

The bill imposes its 15% tax on explicitly charged financial fees and on 'implicit' intermediation — the spread between the basic interest rate and rates paid or charged on accounts and loans — subject to a $10,000 de minimis exemption, while also repealing the corporate income tax those firms currently pay.

Home purchases would become subject to the 15% tax, with the option to pay it in equal annual installments over 30 years plus interest, and the unpaid balance due if the home is sold or stops being a principal residence.

States that adopt a conforming sales tax would administer and collect the federal tax and keep a 1% administration fee, and the multistate vendor program would route multistate retailers' collections through the federal government.
